title: Scope and Local Variables
description: Where a variable exists, how long it lives, and why that keeps big programs manageable.

items: A variable declared inside a method exists only there, from its declaration down to the closing brace.
That region is its **scope**. A variable like this is called a **local** variable.
So two methods can each have a `total`, and the two have nothing to do with each other.

steps.note: Call `show`. Inside it, `main`'s `total` cannot be seen at all.
`show` ended, so its `total` is gone. `main`'s was never touched.

content.title: Two totals, two scopes
content.outro: No method can reach into another's variables, so a mistake in one method cannot quietly break the rest.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `change` sets its own local `x` to 2. `main`'s `x` is a different variable and stays 1.

items: Scope is about braces, not just methods. Every `{ }` makes a new scope, including an `if` or a `for` block.
Declare each variable in the **smallest** block that needs it. A variable you can see from far away can be broken from far away.

items.title: Inside: fine
items.text: `doubled` is used inside the block where it was declared.

items.title: Outside: compile error
items.text: The block ended at `}`, and `doubled` went with it.

content.title: Inside vs outside the block
content.caption: The error is `cannot find symbol`. Outside the braces, `doubled` simply does not exist.
Both loops use `i` happily: the first `i` is gone before the second is born. `biggest` works because it is declared **outside** the loop, the accumulator rule from Module 5.

content.question: Where must `count` be declared to print it after the loop?
content.explain: A variable lives until the closing brace of the block it was declared in. To survive the loop, it must be declared before it.

items.title: cannot find symbol
items.text: From `show`'s point of view there is no `total`. The error says `symbol: variable total`.

items.title: Pass it in
items.text: A parameter gives `show` its own copy to use.

content.title: Use a parameter, not another method's variable

content.value: Seeing `cannot find symbol` for a variable? Ask in order: Is it declared in this method? Did I declare it inside an `if` or `for` I am now outside of? Is it another method's variable, which needs a parameter?
content.title: Three questions

content.caption: Parameters are local too: a local variable that arrives with a value. `countdown` counts its `n` down to 0, and `main`'s `n` never moves.

content.value: Locals are created when a method starts and destroyed when it ends. So a local cannot remember anything between calls.

steps.note: A brand new `visits` is born at 0.
The method ended and `visits` died. Second call.

content.title: Why it never counts past 1
content.outro: Three calls, three brand new variables, three 1s. This catches everybody once.

content.caption: The fix for now: keep the count in `main`. Pass it in, hand it back, assign it. In Module 8, **fields** (variables that belong to the whole class) can remember between calls.

content.question: What does the third call print?
content.explain: `c` is local, so every call starts it again at 0 and adds one.

items: One thing can usefully sit outside every method: a **constant**, written `static final` just inside the class.
Every method can see it, and `final` means nothing can change it. Names in SHOUTY_CASE, as in Module 2.
The rule from now on: constants may be shared. Changing values are passed in and handed back.

parts.label: shared, fixed
parts.note: Belongs to the class, so every method sees it. `final` means it never changes.

parts.label: name
parts.note: SHOUTY_CASE marks it as a constant.

content.caption: Changing the pass mark is a one-line edit that every method picks up, and no method can change it by accident.

The Module 5 score board, split into methods. `main` now reads like a description of the program. `average` refuses to divide by zero, so the guard lives in the one method that needs it. Sample run: `2`, then `85` and `30` prints `85 | ********`, `pass`, `30 | ***`, `fail`, `Average: 57.5`. Next module: arrays, one variable holding a whole list of scores.

quiz.question: Where does a variable declared inside a method exist?
options: Only inside that method, from its declaration to the closing brace
quiz.explain: That is its scope. Two methods can each have a `total` and they are unrelated.

quiz.question: A method tries to use a variable belonging to main. What happens?
options: `cannot find symbol` at compile time: pass it in as a parameter instead
It works, because main runs first
It compiles but the value is 0
quiz.explain: From inside the other method there is genuinely no such variable. A parameter is how a value crosses that boundary.

quiz.question: Why can two `for` loops in the same method both declare `int i`?
options: Each loop's i belongs to that loop's block and is gone before the next starts
Java allows duplicate names for counters
Only if the loops count differently
quiz.explain: Every pair of braces makes a scope, so the first `i` no longer exists when the second is declared.

quiz.question: A method declares `int visits = 0;` then increments and prints it. Called three times, what does it print?
quiz.explain: Locals are created fresh on every call. To carry a value across calls, pass it in and return it, until fields arrive in Module 8.

quiz.question: What may reasonably be declared outside every method, at class level?
options: A `static final` constant that every method can read but none can change
Any variable you want several methods to share
quiz.explain: Constants are safe to share because nothing can change them. Changing values should travel as parameters and return values.
